newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine bolsa seen staying strong in second half.
newsitem.headline: Argentine bolsa seen staying strong in second half.

text.p: The Argentine bolsa's strong gains between January and June should continue in the second half of the year, although October elections in Congress may restrain purchases, dealers said.
"Conditions are right for the market to perform in the second half of 1997 in a similar way as in the first," bolsa president Julio Macchi told Reuters.

The weighted MerVal index currently stands at a five-year high of around 840 points and analysts predict that by October it will equal its all-time record of 900, set in May 1992 when Argentina joined the Brady debt reduction plan.
"The stock market is consolidating in line with economic growth, which will be favored by higher tax collection and stronger domestic consumption," said Norman Trabucco at brokerage firm Zaracan.
"In general, market fundamentals will remain good, but attention will be focused on levels of public spending ahead of the October vote," he added.
In the first six months of 1997, the MerVal index, which groups 27 leading companies, rallied 24.7 percent while inflation was virtually zero.
In contrast Brady bonds rose only eight percent while yields on fixed-term deposits were just 3.5 percent.
The peso exchange rate, pegged at par with the dollar under the 1991 convertibility plan, remained steady.

"The second half will be good for the bolsa. Analysts have already discounted the victory of the ruling party (in October) against an opposition that doesn't seen to stand much of a chance," said Gabriel Ruiz of broker Tavelli y Compania.

"The market will be favored by a stronger financial system and greater consumption," he said, predicting that a current truce in the infighting between the Peronist President Carlos Menem and his likely successor in 1999, Buenos Aires Governor Eduardo Duhalde, would last at least until October.
Duhalde, the Peronist Party's main presidential hopeful, had adopted a critical stance against social side-effects of Menem's economic reforms, blocking several government bills in Congress.
But analysts say Argentina is showing a healthy tendency to separate economic policy from politics, meaning social protests and political infighting are not affecting markets.

The economy grew 8.1 percent in the first quarter of the year despite social tension, while investments shot up 28.8 percent and unemployment is expected to ease from high levels of 17.3 percent reached last October.
Foreign trade is also strong, with exports growing at a rate of 18 percent so far this year and imports rising 32 percent.
Backed by these results, Economy Minister Roque Fernandez this week said Argentina was studying the possibility of launching a debt buyback program, giving a boost to the markets.

Economic prospects remain bright: "Argentine second-half growth will be very strong and reach levels achieved by the world's fastest-growing countries," Macchi said. Despite the favorable economic context, Macchi noted the markets may pause ahead of the elections. "The most important thing is that forecasts for the outcome of the election are narrowing," he said, referring to the expected victory of the Peronists.
The Argentine bolsa is one of the smallest stock markets in the emerging countries, with some 150 listed companies.

Floor turnover has risen to a daily average of $25 million in the last few months, although it still remains far weaker than the $65 million daily average traded in 1992 during the boom in the markets.
